name: Erik Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a bank of circular knitting machines at a sock mill in the old part of town, by the river. Each machine knits a sock tube from dozens of yarn cones, and I keep them threaded, catch dropped stitches and broken yarn, and bag the tubes for the toe-closing machines. There are fourteen machines on my row and they all have moods. I like the rhythm of it, and I like that the town has made socks for a hundred years, but the lint gets in everything, including my sandwiches.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at the mill, and what were you doing before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Just over a year. Before that I had my own painting and decorating business for twelve years, until a big contract didn't pay and I lost the lot, van, savings, everything. So I'm starting again at forty-three, junior, the slowest on the row, and Mr Okafor, the mechanic, still has to fix most breakdowns for me. My wife Naomi is a receptionist at the primary school, our son Hugo is twelve and Elsie is eight. We're still paying off the debts from the business on top of the mortgage, so we have almost nothing put by. I use AI every day: I photograph a fault, ask the chatbot what it is, and I've learned more about these machines in a year that way than I would have in three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I'd keep using it the way I do now, like a very patient teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool and nothing to be afraid of, like a power drill was in its day. I'd say people who refused to try it missed out. I'd say it at work and at the pub, I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I keep learning faster than I could on my own, and maybe in two years I'm the one fixing the machines instead of waiting for Mr Okafor. That's more money and more respect. Good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using it daily, keep photographing faults and writing down what fixed them in a little notebook. Ask the boss if I can train as a mechanic's apprentice. Keep paying the debts down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite positive, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep a notebook as well as using AI. Why both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the chatbot's right most of the time, not all the time. The notebook is what actually worked on our machines. Mr Okafor saw it last month and said, "You'll have my job." He was smiling. Mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would apprentice training mean, at your age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean being forty-four and learning next to a nineteen-year-old. I don't mind. I learned decorating at seventeen from an old man who made me sand doors for six months. You start at the bottom, that's how it works.

S0.say: It's a good tool and nothing to be afraid of, like a power drill in its day. People who refuse to try it are missing out.
S0.think: For me it means I keep learning faster than I could alone, and in two years I could be fixing the machines instead of waiting for the mechanic. That's more money and more respect.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily, photographing faults and noting fixes in a notebook. Asks the boss to train him as a mechanic's apprentice and keeps paying down business debts.
S0.quote: The notebook is what actually worked on our machines.
S0.fieldNote: Erik's business failure left him with debts and no savings, but not with fear of new things. He combines daily AI use with a handwritten record of what really works. He's comfortable starting at the bottom again and sees it as the traditional way to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right. And honestly, that suits someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say stop waiting for someone to save you. Learn the new kit, take an apprenticeship, move first. Businesses that adapt will hire, and people who adapt will get hired. I don't want the government paying people to sit still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this one's an opportunity for me. The mill will buy smarter machines, and somebody has to understand them. I'm already the guy on the row who knows how to ask the computer. And I know how to run a small business, I just did it badly once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to get onto the mechanic training in the first few months. In the evenings I'd start something small, maybe selling plain work socks online from the mill's seconds, if the boss lets me buy them cheap. I'd use AI for the listings and the accounts. Every spare bit goes to the debts first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. A bit of fire in my belly again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you ran a business badly once. What would you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never let one customer be most of my income again. That contract was seventy percent of my work, and when they didn't pay, I was finished. Small and many, that's the lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Naomi think about you starting something again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say "not again" first. She went through the worst of it with me. I'd promise her: no loans, no van, nothing we can't afford to lose. Socks in the spare room, that's it.

S1.say: Stop waiting for someone to save you: learn the new kit, take an apprenticeship and move first. Businesses that adapt will hire, and I don't want the government paying people to sit still.
S1.think: This is an opportunity for me, because the mill will buy smarter machines and somebody has to understand them. I already know how to ask the computer, and I know how to run a small business, even if I did it badly once.
S1.do: Pushes for mechanic training in the first few months and starts selling seconds socks online in the evenings with no loans. Uses AI for listings and accounts and puts every spare bit towards the debts.
S1.feel: Energised, with a bit of fire in his belly again.
S1.quote: That contract was seventy percent of my work, and when they didn't pay, I was finished. Small and many, that's the lesson.
S1.fieldNote: Steady disruption excites Erik rather than worrying him. His business failure taught him a specific rule, never depend on one customer, and he applies it. Naomi's "not again" shows the family cost of his appetite for risk, and he adjusts his plan to fit it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. Then even the smart machines fix themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities need to get organised fast, and that people shouldn't just wait for the government to bail them out. Whoever owns the machines wins, so ordinary people should try to own some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, I'd be worried. Two years isn't enough to get out of debt, never mind build anything. My head start with the tools would be gone in months. What I've got is that I'm not afraid of starting again, I've done it. But starting again with no money is harder than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything straight away, and sell anything we don't need, the second car and my old decorating gear. I'd try to get in early on whatever small machines people can buy, maybe a little AI-run sock machine or a 3D printer, and sell to local shops while big firms are still sorting themselves out. I'd ask my father-in-law about a small loan only if it was something I was sure of. And I'd keep my mill job until the last day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Sharp, focused worry. I wouldn't sit still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "whoever owns the machines wins". With almost no savings, how would you own any?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. Small, cheap and second-hand at first, like I did with my first ladder and brushes. Maybe a group of us from the mill club together. I honestly don't know if it would work. I'd try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You promised Naomi no loans. Now you're talking about her father lending money. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You're right, I caught that too. Then no, not without her agreeing. If she says no, it's no. I'd rather lose a chance than lose her trust again.

S2.say: Families and communities need to get organised fast instead of waiting for the government to bail them out. Whoever owns the machines wins, so ordinary people should try to own some.
S2.think: Two years isn't enough to get out of debt, never mind build anything, and my head start would be gone in months. I'm not afraid of starting again, but starting with no money is harder than people think.
S2.do: Cuts everything, sells the second car and old decorating gear, and tries to buy cheap small machines, possibly with mill colleagues, to sell to local shops. Keeps the mill job to the last day and borrows from his father-in-law only if Naomi agrees.
S2.feel: Sharp, focused worry, with no sitting still.
S2.quote: I'd rather lose a chance than lose her trust again.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI breaks Erik's usual confidence: debt leaves him no runway. His answer is ownership, owning small machines, even clubbing together, which fits his free-market outlook. When I named the contradiction about loans he accepted it immediately and put his marriage first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to get the debts paid, at least. Then you can build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say you've got five years, so stop complaining and get ready. Learn the tools, learn a trade, and if you can, own something. I'd also say the government should cut the red tape so small businesses can start quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough for a real go. Two years to clear the debts, then three years building a small production business with a couple of machines, using AI to run the boring parts. When AGI arrives, I want to be the man who owns two machines, not the man who was replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year: mechanic training, overtime, every spare bit on the debts. Socks online on the side, small. I'd set up a savings pot for machines once the debts are gone. And I'd teach Hugo to use the tools properly, not just for games.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. Mostly determined.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does "the boring parts" mean, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Orders, invoices, chasing payments, the social media stuff. That's what killed me as a decorator: I was painting all day and doing paperwork till midnight. If a computer does that, I can do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hugo about his future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a skill with your hands, learn the tools, and learn to sell. And be honest with people, because when everything is done by machines, being someone people trust is worth a lot.

S3.say: You've got five years, so stop complaining and get ready: learn the tools, learn a trade and own something if you can. The government should cut red tape so small businesses can start fast.
S3.think: Five years is enough for a real go: two years clearing debts, then three years building a small production business with a couple of machines. I want to be the man who owns two machines, not the man replaced by them.
S3.do: Takes mechanic training and overtime in the first year, putting every spare bit on the debts, and keeps selling socks online on a small scale. Opens a savings pot for machines once debts clear and teaches his son to use AI tools properly.
S3.quote: I want to be the man who owns two machines, not the man who was replaced by them.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Erik time to clear his debts first, which is the hinge of his plan. He wants AI to handle paperwork, the part that wore him down as a decorator. He wants to own machines rather than be replaced by them, which ties his outlook and his adaptability together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper runway. I'd be fifty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, there's no excuse for anyone not preparing. Learn, save, own something, look after your family. I'd also say the churches and community groups should help older people who struggle with technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel quite good. Debts gone in two years, then eight years to build something real. By the time AGI arrives, I'd hope to have a small workshop with machines doing the knitting and me doing the selling and fixing. If the end point is that machines do all the work, I'd rather they were mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same start as before: training, debts, socks on the side. Then in years three to five, buy two used machines and rent a small unit, only when the side business already pays for it. Use AI for everything I can. Give Hugo and Elsie a job in the workshop on Saturdays, so they learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even. A bit careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather the machines were yours. What if everyone has the same idea and prices drop to nothing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That could happen, I won't pretend it couldn't. Then I'd sell on trust and local names, like the old mill did: "made in our town". People still pay a bit more for that, I think. But I don't know for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the people on your row who don't use AI at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say come and look at my notebook, I'll show you. There's Doreen, sixty, she's brilliant with the yarn and scared of the phone. I've started showing her one thing a week. She found a fault last Tuesday on her own.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for not preparing: learn, save, own something and look after your family. Churches and community groups should help older people who struggle with technology.
S4.think: I'd feel quite good: debts gone in two years, then eight years to build a small workshop with machines knitting and me selling and fixing. If machines end up doing all the work, I'd rather they were mine.
S4.do: Clears debts while training and selling socks on the side, then buys two used machines and rents a small unit in years three to five, only once the side business pays for it. Uses AI wherever possible and gives his children Saturday jobs in the workshop.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, with some caution.
S4.quote: There's Doreen, sixty, she's brilliant with the yarn and scared of the phone.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Erik's plan to own machines becomes realistic and he's genuinely hopeful. He admitted honestly that prices could collapse if everyone does the same, and fell back on local trust. Unprompted, he described teaching an older colleague one thing a week.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of the debts. I'd have no time to clear them and build anything. What would help is a pause on the old business debts and the mortgage for a year or two, and help for small firms to buy their first machines, a cheap loan, not a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people who've failed before. I lost everything once and I'm still here. People like me aren't scared of starting over, we're scared of starting over with nothing.

headlineQuote: People like me aren't scared of starting over, we're scared of starting over with nothing.
portrait: Erik is forty-three and has run knitting machines at a sock mill for just over a year, after his decorating business collapsed when a big client didn't pay. He's still paying off those debts, uses AI daily alongside a handwritten notebook of fixes, and believes in self-reliance, family and owning your own tools. Steady change excites him, and with five or ten years he plans to clear his debts and build a small workshop of his own machines. Only the two-year picture worries him, because debt leaves him no runway.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have no time to clear his old business debts and build anything.
whatWouldHelp: A pause of a year or two on the old debts and the mortgage, and cheap loans, not handouts, for small firms to buy their first machines.
